  Sirs/महोदय, 
In continuation of our earlier letter dated 03.08.2026 and pursuant to Regulations 30 and 34 of SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, please find attached Annual Report for the financial year 
2025-26 including Notice of 50th AGM of the Company scheduled to be held on Friday, August 28, 2026 at 11:30 A.M. 
(IST) through Video Conference (VC)/ Other Audio Visual Means (OAVM). 
 
 The aforesaid Annual Report including Notice of 50th AGM is also available on the website of Company at the link 
https://www.nhpcindia.com/assests/pzi_public/gallery/17859081100.pdf . 
 
The Company is providing remote e-Voting facility to all its members to cast their votes on all resolutions as set 
out in the Notice of the 50th AGM. Remote e-Voting period commences on Tuesday, 25th August, 2026 at 9:00 AM (IST) 
and ends on Thursday, 27th August, 2026 at 5:00 PM (IST). During this period, members of the Company, holding 
shares either in physical form or in dematerialized form, as on the cut-off date i.e. Friday, 21st August, 2026, shall be 
entitled to avail the facility of remote e-Voting. Further, e-Voting facility shall also be available at the AGM for members (as 
on cut-off date) who had not cast their votes through remote e-Voting. The details regarding manner of registering/updating 
e-mail address, casting vote through e-Voting/remote e-Voting, attending AGM through VC/OAVM have been set out in the 
notice of 50th AGM. 
 
 This is for your information and record.

Industry Outlook
India's power sector stands at a defining juncture. 
The 
nation's 
commitment 
to 
achieving 
500 
GW 
of 
non-fossil fuel 
capacity 
by

ability to provide grid balancing, peaking 
support and round-the-clock storage through 
pumped storage projects, is being recognised 
afresh as the natural complement to India's 
rapidly expanding solar and wind capacity.
Government initiatives such as the Hydro

legacy projects, budgetary support for enabling 
infrastructure in the Himalayan and North-

Storage Projects (PSPs) as the storage backbone 
of the grid, are creating a conducive environment 
for capacity addition. NHPC, as the country's premier 
hydropower developer, is well positioned to capture

wind and green hydrogen, in line with its stated vision 
of becoming a fully diversified green energy major.

Our Golden Jubilee Journey
On 7th November 2025, NHPC completed fifty glorious 
years of service to the nation, marking its 51st Raising 
Day. What began in 1975 as National Hydroelectric 
Power Corporation Private Limited, with the modest 
task of executing the Salal, Bairasiul and Loktak projects, 
has today grown into one of the largest hydropower 
organisations in the world, with capabilities spanning 
investigation, design, construction and operation of 
large and small hydro projects across some of the most 
challenging Himalayan terrains.
The Golden Jubilee was commemorated with befitting 
solemnity and pride. The Hon'ble Union Minister of Power, 
Housing & Urban Affairs released a special commemorative 
₹50 coin and a customised 'My Stamp' issued by India 
Post featuring twelve of our iconic dams and barrages, 
along with an 'Achievement Book' chronicling five 
decades of milestones, technological excellence and 
contribution to nation-building. Grand celebrations 
were held simultaneously at our Corporate Office in 
Faridabad and across all Regional Offices, Power Stations 
and Project sites, bringing together employees, families 
and stakeholders in shared celebration of this landmark. 
This jubilee year is not merely a commemoration of our 
past; it is a renewal of our commitment to the next fifty 
years - years in which NHPC aims to lead India's transition 
to a secure, diversified and green energy future, working 
towards our aspiration of 50,000 MW installed capacity by 
2047.

Completion of 50 years of establishment and 
celebration of the Golden Jubilee on November 7, 
2025.

year - 1850 MW - through commissioning of the 
Subansiri Lower (750 MW), Parbati-II (800 MW) and 
Karnisar Solar (300 MW) projects.
	
Consolidated installed capacity, together with 
subsidiaries and joint ventures, crossed 9333 MW 
from 31 power stations, with a further 17 projects 
aggregating 9204 MW under construction.

Continued progress on the Company's pipeline of 
Pumped Storage Projects and diversification into 
solar, wind and green hydrogen.

financial strength.

Operating Performance Highlights
On a standalone basis, our power stations achieved 
generation of 23307 Million Units during FY 2025-26, 
from an installed capacity of 7401 MW across 25 power 
stations. This performance was achieved despite the 
inherent hydrology-related variability of river flows, and 
reflects the continued focus of our operations teams 
on plant availability, efficient reservoir management 
and preventive maintenance. The commissioning of the 
Subansiri Lower and Parbati-II projects during the year, 
together with the Karnisar Solar project, represented 
the highest capacity addition achieved by the Company 
in any single fiscal year of its history, a testament to the 
sustained execution capabilities we have built over five 
decades.
We continued to make steady progress across our 
under-construction portfolio, while advancing survey, 
investigation and clearance activities on a further pipeline 
of projects that will underpin capacity growth in the years 
ahead.
Financial Performance Highlights
NHPC delivered a strong financial performance in FY 
2025-26. On a consolidated basis, total income for the 
year rose to ₹12,686.09 crore, compared to ₹11,614.61 
crore in the previous year, while consolidated net profit for 
the year increased to ₹4,220.46 crore, up from ₹3,411.73 
crore in FY 2024-25. Performance in the fourth quarter 
was particularly strong, with consolidated net profit rising 
over 68% year-on-year to ₹1,549.42 crore on total income 
of ₹3,120.52 crore, aided by improved generation and a 
favourable resolution of certain tax matters.
On a standalone basis, net profit for the full year stood 
at ₹3,617.80 crore, an increase of 17.31% over ₹3,083.98 
crore in the previous year. In recognition of this 
performance, the Board of Directors has recommended 
a final dividend of ₹0.21 per equity share, in addition 
to the interim dividend of ₹1.40 per share already paid 
during the year, taking the total dividend for FY 2025-26 
to ₹1.61 per equity share. The Board has also approved 
fund-raising up to ₹10,000 crore during FY 2025-26 
through Secured/ Unsecured  Corporate Bonds and/
or Term Loans/ External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), 
out of which the Company has raised ₹3,854.33 crore 
through term loan/ monetization facilities, ₹3,945 
crore through non-convertible bonds to support the

Shri Bhupender Gupta has taken over the charge of the post of Chairman & Managing 
Director of NHPC Limited, India’s premier hydropower Company and a Navratna Enterprise 
of Government of India on 04.09.2025. He is also Chairman on the Boards of NHDC Limited 
and Loktak Downstream Hydroelectric Corporation Limited (Subsidiary Companies of 
NHPC Limited). Shri Gupta is also holding the additional charge of the post of Chairman 
& Managing Director, SJVN Limited, a Navratna Enterprise of Government of India, since 1st May 2025. He is also 
Chairman on the Boards of SJVN Arun-3 Power Development Company Private Limited and SJVN Lower Arun Power 
Development Company Private Limited (Wholly-Owned Subsidiaries of SJVN Limited). Shri Bhupender Gupta holds a 
bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and an MBA in Operations Management. He began his professional career 
with ACC Ltd. in 1991 and started his CPSU career by joining SJVN in 1995, where he served for 12 years in various 
positions. During this period, he was responsible for the planning, erection and commissioning as well as O&M of the 
electromechanical equipment of the 1500 MW Nathpa Jhakri Hydro Power Plant, the largest operational hydroelectric 
project in India. He also served on deputation in Bhutan with the 1020 MW Tala Hydroelectric Power Project for around 
three years (2002–2005).
Subsequently, he joined REC Ltd. in March 2007 and was associated with project financing of Hydro, Thermal projects 
for approximately 6 years. Thereafter, he worked as Additional Chief Executive Officer (CEO) in two subsidiaries of REC 
i.e. REC Transmission Projects Co. Ltd. and REC Power Distribution Co. Ltd. as the Operational Head. During his tenure, he 
oversaw execution, project management, contract management and consultancy for power sector projects across Pan 
India & successfully completed Govt. of India Flagship scheme assigned to REC i.e. Saubhagya, Deen Dayal Upadhyaya 
Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY), PMDP etc.
Shri Gupta later joined as Director (Technical) at the Punatsangchhu Hydroelectric Project Authority, in Bhutan 
in December 2020 on deputation and spearheaded on-going construction activities and resolved long pending 
contractual & pending issues. Thereafter, Shri Gupta joined THDCIL as Director (Technical) on 9th June 2023. Shri Gupta 
provided strategic leadership in addressing commissioning challenges and Covid-19 impacts, facilitating THDCIL in 
successfully achieving CoD of 1320 MW of Khurja STPP. Shri Gupta guided Civil, HM and EM teams in resolving major civil 
challenges, pump-turbine operational issues and commissioning hurdles due to implementing advanced technology 
(VSI) in Tehri PSP, leading to successful CoD of Unit-1 & 2 (250 MW each) of Tehri PSP. He also steered the redeployment 
of stalled operation of Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM) in 444 MW Vishnugad Pipalkoti HEP and now the project is in 
advance stage of completion. After assigned additional charge of CMD SJVN from 1/5/2025, he provided strategic 
leadership in addressing commissioning challenges of Buxar Thermal PP and facilitated successful achieving CoD of 
first Unit in Sep’25 (660 MW) and Second Unit is in advanced stage of commissioning. SJVNL has also commissioned 
entire capacity of 1000 MW Bikaner Solar Power Project in Dec’2025, under his leadership.
After taking charge as CMD NHPC, Shri Gupta is actively steering NHPC towards faster execution and commissioning 
of ongoing projects and bringing new hydro projects in the NHPC portfolio. Since taking over the charge of NHPC, 
commissioning of 300 MW Bikaner Solar Plant and COD of four units of Subansiri Lower HEP of 250 MW each has been

With an illustrious career spanning more than 34 years including 31 years in Power CPSUs, Shri Gupta has contributed 
significantly to the Indian power sector across hydro, thermal, renewable energy, transmission and distribution 
domains. His contribution encompassed planning, design, execution, contract and project management and O&M of 
large hydro projects as well as transmission and distribution projects.
Shri Gupta’s future vision focuses on addressing India’s growing power demand through non-fossil fuel-based 
resources, with the aim of making our country self-reliant in energy security. The vision also emphasizes meeting 
sustainable energy targets through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), along with the adoption of other new 
and emerging technologies such as: EV integration into the grid, cybersecurity and digital protection, green hydrogen, 
bioenergy and energy storage.

15.	 TDS ON DIVIDEND 
	
1.	
As per Income Tax Act, 2025 (as amended by 
Finance Act, 2026) (“IT Act”), dividend paid and 
distributed by the Company is taxable in the 
hands of shareholders in accordance with the 
provisions of the IT Act. In this connection, the 
shareholders are requested to take note of the 
following:
A.	
Resident Shareholders:
	
(i)	
Tax will be deducted at source ("TDS") under 
Section 393(1) [Table: S. No. 7] of the Act @ 10% 
on the amount of dividend paid or distributed 
by the company during the Tax Year 2026-27, 
unless exempt under any of the provisions of 
the Act.
	
(ii)	
However, in case of individual shareholders, 
TDS would not apply if the aggregate of total 
dividend distributed to them by the Company 
during the Tax year 2026-27 does not 
exceed ₹10,000. For non-individual resident 
shareholders (companies, firms, LLPs, etc.), TDS 
is applicable without any monetary threshold.
	
(iii)	 TDS will also not be deducted where a 
shareholder submits a duly signed Form No. 
121 (prescribed under Section 393(6) of the 
IT Act read with Rule 211 of the Income-tax 
Rules, 2026), which replaces the erstwhile 
Form No. 15G and Form No. 15H. Form No. 
121 may be submitted by eligible resident 
individual shareholders (including those aged 
60 years and above), provided the eligibility 
conditions are met. HUFs are not eligible to 
submit Form No. 121 for claiming nil TDS on 
dividend income. Blank Form No. 121 can be 
downloaded from the following link:-
	
	
https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/
documents/d/guest/form-no-121-1
	
(iv)	 The Central Board of Direct Taxes ("CBDT") has 
revised Form 121, incorporating additional 
disclosures. Accordingly, shareholders are 
requested to carefully review the revised 
requirements and ensure that all columns 
are duly completed in the updated Form 121. 
Further, shareholders are required to fully 
complete Part-A (including the declaration 
therein) and Part-B (Sr. Nos. 8,9, 11 to 18 only). 
Please note that all fields mentioned in the 
forms are mandatory and the Company may 
reject the forms submitted, if not filled up 
correctly.
	
(v)	
NIL / lower tax will be deducted on dividend 
payable to the following categories of 
resident shareholders, on submission of self-
declarations:
	
	
a.	
Insurance Companies: Declaration that 
the provisions of Section 393(4) [Table: 
S.No.10] of the IT Act are applicable, along 
with self-attested copy of registration 
certificate and PAN card;
	
	
b.	
Mutual Funds: Declaration by the 
mutual fund as specified under Schedule 
VII [Table: Sl. No. 20 or 21] to Section 11 of 
the IT Act along with self-attested copies 
of the registration documents and PAN 
card;
	
	
c.	
AIF established in India: Declaration 
that the shareholder is eligible for 
exemption under Schedule V [Table: 
Sl. No. 1] to Section 11 of the IT Act and 
that they are established as Category 
I or Category II AIF under the Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (Alternative 
Investment Fund) Regulations, 2012, 

24
Annual Report 2025-26
made under the Securities and Exchange 
Board of India Act, 1992. Copy of self-
attested registration documents and PAN 
card should also be provided;
	
	
d.	
New Pension System Trust: Declaration 
along 
with 
self-attested 
copy 
of 
documentary evidence supporting the 
exemption under Schedule VII (41) to 
Section 11 of the IT Act and self-attested 
copy of PAN card;
	
	
e.	
Recognized Provident Fund/ Approved 
Superannuation 
Fund/ 
Approved 
Gratuity Fund: Self-declaration that its 
income is eligible for exemption under 
Schedule VII [22,23,24] to Section 11 of 
the IT Act along with self-attested copy 
of PAN card and approval granted by 
Commissioner of Income Tax;
	
	
f.	
Corporation established by or under 
a Central Act which is, under any law 
for the time being in force, exempt 
from income-tax on its income: Self-
declaration 
specifying 
the 
specific 
Central Act under which such corporation 
is established and that their income is 
exempt under the provisions of the IT 
Act along with a self-attested copy of the 
PAN card and registration certificate.
	
	
g.	
Dividend payable to Government, 
Reserve Bank or certain corporations: 
No TDS is required to be deducted as per 
Section 393(5) of the IT Act;
	
	
h.	
Other shareholders: Declaration along 
with self-attested copy of documentary 
evidence supporting the exemption and 
self-attested copy of PAN card;
	
	
i.	
Certificate for lower/Nil deduction: 
Shareholders who have provided a 
valid certificate issued u/s 395(1) of the 
IT Act for lower / nil rate of deduction 
or an exemption certificate issued by 
the income tax authorities along with 
Declaration.
	
	
Application of Nil rate at the time of tax 
deduction / withholding on dividend amounts 
will depend upon the completeness and 
satisfactory review by the Company of the 
documents submitted by such shareholders.
	
(vi)	 However, TDS shall be deducted at higher rates 
as stated below in the following circumstances: 
	
	
•	
Valid PAN not available: If a valid PAN 
is not registered with the Company's 
Register of Members, TDS shall be 
deducted at 20% as per Section 397(2) of 
the IT Act.
	
	
•	
Inoperative PAN: As per Section 262(6) 
of the IT Act, every person who has been 
allotted a PAN and who is eligible to 
obtain Aadhaar, shall be required to link 
the PAN with Aadhaar. In case of failure 
to comply to this, the PAN allotted shall 
be deemed to be invalid/inoperative and 
tax shall be deducted at the rate of 20% 
as per the provisions of Section 397(2) 
of the IT Act. The Company will be using 
online functionality of the Income tax 
department for the above purpose and 
no claim shall lie against the Company 
if tax is deducted based on the status on 
the said online functionality of Income 
Tax department.
	
	
The above provision makes it mandatory on 
part of the Company to withhold taxes in all 
cases where the amount of dividend likely to 
be paid during the relevant tax year exceeds 
.10,000/-. NHPC has been regularly paying 
interim and final dividend since last few 
years and it is expected that the Company 
would pay an interim dividend during the 
current year also i.e., financial year 2026-27. 
Accordingly, TDS will be deducted @10% on 
the final dividend for financial year 2025-26 
with a threshold limit of .8,000/-.

NHPC Limited is a Navratna Central Public Sector 
Enterprise of Government of India with an authorized 
share capital of .17,500 crore and is a Listed Company. 
NHPC is one of the top hydro power developers in India 
with over 51 years of experience in hydro power sector. 
NHPC has successfully developed twenty-two hydro 
power stations, two solar power projects and one wind 
power project across the Country. At present, NHPC is 
engaged in the construction of various hydro-electric and 
solar projects. Further, various hydro-electric, solar and 
pumped storage projects are under pipeline, details of 
which already forms part of the Directors’ Report. NHPC 
is in rapid capacity addition mode by taking projects of 
different sources of energy i.e. hydro (including PSP), 
renewables, etc. These projects are to be financed in 
debt equity ratio of 70:30 as per CERC norms. The main 
constituents of the Company’s borrowings are generally 
in the form of bonds/ debentures, rupee term loans 
from banks and financial institutions, foreign currency 
borrowings, subordinate debts from Govt. of India etc. 
As per the requirements of Section 180(1)(c) of the Act, 
the shareholders of the Company by a special resolution 
passed in 49th Annual General Meeting held on August 
30, 2025 had authorized Board of Directors to borrow 
upto .60,000 crore in excess of paid up share capital, free 
reserves and security premium account. Keeping in view 
of fund requirements due to very robust CAPEX plan of 
the Company, the limit of .60,000 crore is required to 
be increased. The tentative debt requirement for both 
ongoing projects and new projects up to about next five 
years as per CAPEX requirements will be approx. .67,500 
crore, which will exceed the approved borrowing limit of 
.60,000 crore in about next three years. In view of the 
above, approval of the Shareholders of the Company is 
being sought by way of Special Resolution, for authorizing

DIRECTORS’ REPORT
Dear Members,
The Board of Directors of your Company takes pleasure 
in presenting the 50th Annual Report of the Company, 
commemorating five decades of sustained growth, 
commitment, and service. This Report provides an 
overview of the Company's operational and financial 
performance, key developments, and achievements 
during FY 2025–26. The Report is accompanied by the 
audited financial statements for the year ended March 31, 
2026, together with the reports of the Statutory Auditors 
and the Secretarial Auditor, as well as the review of the 
financial statements conducted by the Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India (C&AG).
Major highlights of performance of your Company are as 
under:
	
NHPC has earned Profit After Tax (PAT) of `3,617.80 
crore on standalone basis and `4,220.46 crore on 
consolidated basis.
	
On standalone basis, total income and revenue from 
operations were `11,650.10 crore and `10,328.26 
crore respectively, and total comprehensive income 
and other comprehensive income were `3,542.39 
crore and `(75.41) crore respectively. 
	
NHPC’s power stations recorded overall Plant 
Availability Factor (PAF) of 69.50% and generated 
23306.92 Million Units (MUs) during the year. 
	
Cash contribution of `1,293.10 crore was made to 
Government of India’s exchequer through dividend 
(final dividend for FY 2024-25 of `345.28 crore and 
interim dividend for FY 2025-26 of `947.82 crore) 
during FY 2025-26.
	
Commercial operation of 4 out of 8 units (250 MW 
each) of Subansiri Lower HE Project (2000 MW), 
located in Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, has been 
declared in phased manner up to May, 2026.
	
Under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister 
Shri Narendra Modi, the Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs (CCEA), accorded investment 
approval for implementation of 1720 MW Kamala 
Hydroelectric Project in Arunachal Pradesh.
	
The entire 300 MW of Solar Power Project at Karnisar 
Bhatiyan, District Bikaner, stands commissioned. 
This landmark project stands as a testament to the 
‘Make in India’ initiative, being constructed entirely 
with 100% domestically manufactured Solar PV 
Modules.
	
Another major milestone of daylighting of Diversion 
Tunnel-3 at the 2880 MW Dibang Multipurpose 
Project was successfully achieved during the year.
	
Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi laid 
the foundation stone for the 50 MW Floating Solar 
Project at West Kallada, Kerala. This project, being 
developed under the Solar Park Scheme of the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy represents 
a major step towards India’s clean energy transition.
Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi laid the foundation stone for  
50 MW Floating Solar Project in West Kallada, Kerala.
	
NHPC has once again been honored with the 
prestigious ‘Great Place to Work’ certification by 
Great Place to Work, India-marking the second 
consecutive year of this recognition.
	
NHPC proudly participated in the Bharat Electricity 
Summit 2026, held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi 
showcasing its initiatives in hydropower, renewable 
energy and sustainable infrastructure, alongwith its 
technological advancements and future roadmap.

5.1.1	SUBANSIRI LOWER H.E. PROJECT - 2000 MW (8 X 250 MW), ARUNACHAL PRADESH / ASSAM
The Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project is one of India’s largest run-of-the-river hydroelectric projects. The project is 
located on the Subansiri River, a major tributary of the Brahmaputra, near the border of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. 
After completion, the Project will generate 7422 MUs annually in a 90% dependable year. In addition, the project 
will support regional development by improving infrastructure, creating employment opportunities, and enhancing 
connectivity in remote areas. Strategically, the project is important for strengthening India’s renewable energy portfolio 
and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. It also plays a role in grid stability by providing peaking power. Overall, the 
project represents a key component of hydropower development in the northeastern region and a significant step 
towards sustainable energy generation in the country.
The estimated project cost is `27,948.52 crore. 97.57% physical progress has been achieved till March, 2026. All the 
major works have been completed. The project is in advance stage of commissioning. COD of 4 out of 8 units of 250 
MW each, have been achieved, up to May, 2026. Balance 4 units are expected to be commissioned by March, 2027 in 
phased manner.

several measures to de-carbonize the energy sector, your company is also significantly pivoting its strategy to align 
with India’s intensified push towards the 500 GW RE milestone by 2030. During FY 2025-26, NHPC has commissioned 
its 300 MW Karnisar Solar Power Project under CPSU Scheme at Bikaner, Rajasthan and is making continuous efforts to 
contribute towards GOI’s RE generation targets by exploring all possible opportunities to develop RE projects through 
various modes such as development of Solar/Wind power projects, Solar parks/Floating solar projects, Pilot Green 
Hydrogen Projects, Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Pumped Storage Projects etc. in various potential rich states 
across the country.
NHPC has already incorporated two subsidiary companies for development of RE potential, namely NHPC Renewable 
Energy Limited (NHPC REL) (a wholly owned subsidiary for taking up Renewable Energy, Small Hydro Projects and 
Hydrogen Technology based projects) and Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) (JV with UPNEDA to develop RE

(ANGEL), with Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation Limited (APGENCO) for development of pumped storage 
hydro projects and RE projects (solar/floating solar/wind). 
NHPC has been designated as Renewable Energy Implementing Agency (REIA) by MNRE. NHPC has also been designated 
as BESS Implementing Agency (BIA) to act as intermediary procurer for development of BESS projects anywhere in 
India. As a designated REIA & BIA, NHPC’s role has become very significant towards a facilitator for Renewable & Storage 
capacity addition for the country and an important revenue pillar for the company.

35.1	INDUSTRY STRUCTURE AND DEVELOPMENT
Electricity is among the most invisible yet indispensable 
elements of modern life. Digital public infrastructure, 
smarter networks, and new market arrangements are 
reshaping how electricity is produced, consumed, and 
valued. As these changes continue to take root, electricity 
remains a quiet but essential enabler of growth, inclusion, 
and opportunity. Over the past decade, India’s power 
sector has undergone a period of major structural change 
to ensure reliable, affordable, and universal access to 

82
Annual Report 2025-26
power. As India’s economy grows and living standards 
rise, electricity demand continues to expand across 
households, industry, agriculture, and services. Focusing 
on this, the generation capacity has scaled/ expanded 
steadily across conventional and renewable sources.
India's installed non-fossil fuel capacity has witnessed an 
extraordinary rise that establishes India globally as the 
3rd largest  in total installed renewable energy capacity. 
In a remarkable energy transition, India achieved an 
unprecedented ~50% of its installed electricity capacity 
from non-fossil fuel sources by June 2025 - five years 
ahead of its 2030 Paris Agreement Nationally Determined 
Contribution (NDC) target. As the world repositions 
itself towards sustainability, India's renewable sector 
has unleashed extraordinary growth opportunities, 
positioning the country as a global leader in clean energy 
adoption.1 
India, at COP26 in November 2021, announced its target 
to achieve net zero by 2070, positioning the renewable 
energy sector as a catalyst for vast potential beyond 
creating a cleaner future. Towards this, the government 
has launched several flagship initiatives, including setting-
up of solar parks across multiple states with capacities of 
500 MW or more, PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, 
Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation 
(SATAT) initiative which promotes Compressed Bio-Gas 
(CBG) production plants and forward-looking policies 
including waiver of Inter-State Transmission Charges, 
Renewable Purchase Obligations, Production Linked 
Incentives and budgetary support towards cost of 
enabling infrastructure.
These changes have redefined the industry outlook and 
are enabling the transition of Indian power sector towards 
a more sustainable and competitive future, with a focus 
on renewable energy and efficient grid management. 
The same is also reflected through consistent growth in 
generating capacity. A series of concerted measures led to 
a 93.79 % increase in generation capacity - from 275 GW in 
March, 2015 to ~532.74 GW in March, 2026. The Installed 
Capacity as on March 2026 was 532.74 GW comprising of 
249.27 GW thermal (comprising of Coal, Gas and Diesel), 
8.78 GW Nuclear, 274.68 GW Renewables including large 
hydro of 51.41 GW.2

35.2	STRATEGIC DIVERSIFICATION
NHPC is one of the India’s leading hydro power generation 
company and is considering upcoming opportunities in 
Renewable Energy to reduce dependence on hydropower 
alone and position itself as a comprehensive renewable 
energy player and an integrated clean energy company 
aligned with India’s long-term energy transition goals.  
While retaining its core strength holding a 16% share of 
India's installed hydroelectric capacity with operations 
across 15 States and 2 Union territories.  The diversification 
is a deliberate response to India's energy transition, as 
hydropower alone faces constraints from limited suitable 
sites and growing environmental considerations.  
NHPC had signed MoUs with various state Governments 
for joint development of pump storage and other 
renewable energy projects. The Company's broader 
ambition is to contribute meaningfully to India's target of 
500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. This multi-
pronged strategy anchored in hydropower but branching 
into solar, wind and pumped storage, strengthens NHPC's 
long-term competitiveness and aligns it well with India's 
evolving energy policy landscape.

35.5	GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES FOR RENEWABLE 
ENERGY SECTOR
Amid various challenges, to meet the target of 500 GW 
of renewables by 2030, Govt. of India has taken major 
steps to reform the energy sector and usher in a climate-
friendly energy transition that will deliver energy security, 
affordability, and sustainability. The steps include 
initiatives like PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, PM-KUSUM, 
and National Green Hydrogen Mission, Production Linked 
Incentives (PLI) Scheme for domestic manufacturing of 
High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules, various schemes to 
promote large scale Solar Power Development such as 
CPSU Scheme, Solar Park Scheme and extension in waiver 
of ISTS charges for renewable energy projects.
The planned large scale integration of renewable energy 
in the national grid has made Energy Storage Capacity a 
critical aspect to meet the challenges of flexibility (grid 
support / ancillary service), reliability (fast response / 
ramping up / peaking support) and security. In order to 
enhance grid flexibility, integration of renewable with the 
grid and to meet the peak power demand, Govt. of India 
has also introduced VGF based scheme for Battery Energy 
system through Market component, State component, 
CPSU component and PSDF. In the interest of optimal 
use of Renewable Energy and smooth transition of Indian 
Power Sector to Net Zero by the year 2070, it is essential to 
take up large scale development of Hydro Pumped Storage 
Projects (PSPs) in the country, which will play a vital role in 
Grid balancing by meeting the peak power requirements, 
energy arbitrage, ancillary services, RE smoothing. 
Accordingly, Ministry of Power, Govt. of India on April 10, 
2023 has issued “Guidelines to promote development 
of Pump Storage Projects (PSP)”. The guideline offer that 
PSPs are energy storage schemes, hence PSPs would be 
kept out of the liability of free power, LADF and Upfront 
Premium for Project allocations.  
Above initiatives in the Renewable Energy Sector in 
conjunction with technological advancements have 
made the investment in RE sector highly attractive. 
NHPC is also making its efforts to explore opportunities 
for development of renewable energy and PSP through 
different modes.

 	
Geological uncertainties:
	
Inaccessible terrain and constraints of logistic and 
limits of investigation, poses serious consequences 
for execution of projects. Excavation of tunnels 
under high superincumbent cover also poses 
serious problems in timely completion of projects 
due to severe stress related problems and heavy 
ingress of water. Hydropower plants face significant 
challenges from natural hazards, particularly 
because they are often located in mountainous, 
geologically active regions. Key threats include 
earthquakes, flash floods, landslides, avalanches, 
Landslide Lake Outburst Flood (LLOF) and Glacial 
Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF), which can damage 
infrastructure 
and 
cause 
severe 
operational 
disruptions.
	
 Time and cost overruns 
	
Most hydro-electric projects are generally located 
in hilly terrain, which are at the receiving end of 
devastating natural calamities like landslides, hill 
slope collapses and roadblocks, flood, cloud burst, 
etc. These calamities cause severe setbacks in 
construction schedule. Further, in-spite of extensive 
survey and investigation, geological uncertainties 
may have to be tackled especially in long tunnels 
such as Head Race Tunnel. Often, construction 
of road to project structures becomes difficult 
due to unstable rock conditions, necessitating 
the construction of road tunnels, which adds 
additional costs to the project. NHPC with its rich 
experience and expertise coupled with state-of-the 
art technology has overcome such surprises many 
a times in the past. However, these uncommon 
and unpredictable geological uncertainties may 
result in time and cost overrun. Sometimes law 
and order problems also result in time and cost 
overrun. Volatility in raw material prices and global 
supply chain disruptions for critical components 
like transformers and solar modules also lead to 
significant cost overruns.
	
Time consuming clearance process
	
Before any hydroelectric project is implemented, 
it needs to be cleared by various agencies by 
obtaining various statutory as well as non-statutory 
clearances. Often projects get bogged down with 
the lengthy clearance procedures involving multiple 
agencies/ organizations, states, etc. Obtaining 
the requisite clearances is a complex, tedious and 
time-consuming process which sometimes leads 
to abnormal delay, ultimately affecting the project 
implementation.
	
Difficulties in entering into Power Purchase 
Agreements (PPAs) 
	
Sale of energy from projects having higher tariff 
is getting difficult in present day’s power trading

scenario. Beneficiaries prefer to purchase their 
additional power requirement on short-term basis 
through power exchange or e-procurement rather 
than opting for long term/medium term PPAs. As 
hydroelectric projects are site specific and its tariff 
depends on location/design parameters and high 
initial investment, the tariff for new hydroelectric 
projects is relatively higher. Excessive bidding 
during past 2 years in the Renewable Energy Sector 
has also resulted into supply demand mismatch. 
Further, delayed availability of connectivity and 
declining tariff in subsequent bids due to extreme 
market competitions is putting a lot of challenge 
in securing Power Sale Agreements with Buying 
Entities. Due to above reasons, NHPC is facing 
difficulties in dispatch of power from new projects 
through long term PPAs.
	
High initial cost/ tariff 
	
The development of hydroelectric projects involves 
long gestation period and require large initial 
investment, which results into high initial tariff. Cash 
flow and revenue from operations of hydroelectric 
projects are also subject to variations as per tariff 
regulations notified by CERC from time to time. 
High initial costs and tariffs sometimes prove 
detrimental in obtaining investment sanction and 
require extensive financial re-engineering and 
different waivers from various stakeholders to bring 
the project on the anvil.
	
Law & order and Security Threats
	
NHPC is witnessing law & order problem at some 
of its projects/ power stations, as they are located 
near sensitive border areas and at remote locations. 
Officials posted at those projects/ power stations 
are prone to security threats. However, NHPC is 
efficiently managing the operation of these Power 
Plants.
	
Opposition to hydroelectric projects
	
Hydroelectric projects in India are also facing 
opposition by certain pressure groups. This has 
created an apprehension amongst the hydroelectric 
project developers as some of their projects are 
getting stalled. 
	
Restrictive hydro policies of State Government
	
Several state hydro policies favors for payment 
of upfront premium, free power over & above 
the required free power, etc. for allocation of 
hydroelectric projects to the developers. CPSEs are 
facing difficulties in getting these hydroelectric 
projects, as they have to follow the norms of 
Government of India.
	
Dependence on few contractors
 	
Construction of hydroelectric projects require 
manpower, machinery and substantial investment 
of money. There are very few contractors in India 
who can deliver especially in remote and difficult 
locations where accessibility is a major issue. 
The limited range of contractors who are able to 
perform in the sector increases our dependence on 
few available contractors in the Country.

recoverable from or payable to the beneficiaries.

Joint Venture of NHPC Ltd. (51.08%) and Government

capital of `3,000 crore. NHDC has commissioned Indira 
Sagar Power Project (1,000 MW) and Omkareshwar Power

Loktak Downstream Hydroelectric Corporation Limited 
was incorporated on October 23, 2009 as a Joint Venture

share capital of the Company was `142.65 crore out of

Company is yet to start construction activity.
Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL)
Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited was incorporated on 
February 02, 2015, as a Joint Venture of NHPC Ltd. and 
Government of Uttar Pradesh (UPNEDA), with NHPC’s 
share not less than 74%. The authorized share capital 
of the Company was `450 crore. Paid up share capital 
of the Company was `138.18 crore out of which NHPC’s 
contribution is `125.23 crore (90.63%). The Total Income 
of Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) for FY ended 
March 31, 2026 and 2025 was `30.89 crore and `28.50 
crore respectively. The Profit After Tax of Bundelkhand 
Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) for FY ended March 31, 2026 and 
2025 was `(-)11.69 crore and `(-)4.25 crore respectively. 
The Company is involved in construction of solar projects 
and solar parks in the state of Uttar Pradesh. 
Jalpower Corporation Limited (JPCL)
On March 31, 2021, NHPC had acquired Jalpower 
Corporation Limited under insolvency resolution process 
and the JPCL had become a wholly owned subsidiary of 
NHPC from that date. The acquisition was made as per the 
resolution plan submitted by NHPC and approved by the 
National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). The authorized 
share capital of the Company was `600 crore. Paid up share 
capital of the Company was `533.10 crore. The Company 
is engaged in the construction of the 120 MW Rangit-IV 
Hydroelectric Project in the State of Sikkim. The Company 
is yet to commence commercial operations. The Board of 
Directors of NHPC Limited has approved the proposal for 
the merger of JPCL with NHPC Limited in accordance with 
the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. 
The merger proposal has also received approval from the 
Ministry of Power. The merger process is currently under 
consideration at the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA).
Ratle Hydroelectric Power Corporation Limited

Ratle Hydroelectric Power Corporation Limited was 
incorporated on June 01, 2021, as a Joint Venture of NHPC 
Ltd. and Jammu & Kashmir State Power Development 
Corporation Limited (JKSPDCL), with equity participation 
of 51:49 respectively. The authorized share capital of 
the Company was `1,600 crore. Paid up share capital 
of the Company was `1,584.47 crore of which NHPC’s 
contribution is `808.14 crore (51.00%). The Company 
is engaged in the construction of the 850 MW Ratle 
Hydroelectric Power Project in the Union Territory of 
Jammu & Kashmir. The Company is yet to start operation.
Chenab Valley Power Projects Limited (CVPPL)
Chenab Valley Power Projects Limited (CVPPL) was 
incorporated on June 13, 2011 as a Joint Venture 
Company among NHPC Limited (49%), Jammu & Kashmir 
State Power Development Corporation Limited (JKSPDCL) 
(49%), and PTC India Limited (2%) for the development 
and execution of the Pakal Dul (1000 MW), Kiru (624 
MW), and Kwar (540 MW) Hydroelectric Projects in the 
Chenab River Basin in the Union Territory of Jammu & 
Kashmir. NHPC Limited acquired the 2% equity stake held 
by PTC India Limited in CVPPL during FY 2021-22 for a 
consideration of `4.19 crore, increasing its shareholding 
to 51%. Thereafter, pursuant to the execution of the 
Supplementary Promoters’ Agreement between NHPC 
Limited and Jammu & Kashmir State Power Development 
Corporation Limited on November 21, 2022, NHPC 
Limited obtained majority representation on the Board 
of Directors of CVPPL and acquired control over the 
company with effect from that date. Accordingly, CVPPL 
has been accounted for as a subsidiary of NHPC Limited 
from ibid date.

`8,000 crore. Paid up share capital of the company was 
`5,948.57 crore out of which NHPC’s contribution was

1.	
Brief outline on CSR Policy of the Company:
	
Your Company has a CSR & Sustainability Policy aligned with the provisions of CSR under Section 135 of the 
Companies Act, 2013, the Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Rules 2014, and subsequent 
amendments issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India. The policy outlines the guiding 
principles for the selection, implementation, and monitoring of activities, among others. Your Company also aims 
to adhere to the CSR Guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE). The CSR Policy of your 
Company, broadly includes the following:
	
l	
In terms of Section 135 of Companies Act 2013, the Company shall spend, in every financial year, at least 
two percent of the average net profits made during the three immediately preceding financial years. 
Accordingly, an annual budget for CSR activities is allocated and approved by the Board of Directors based 
on the recommendation of the Committee of Directors on CSR & Sustainability.
	
l	
At least 80% of the CSR schemes/ activities are to be executed in and around NHPC’s Projects, Power Stations 
and offices preferably within 25 km and in the district where the project is located. However, other locations 
may also be chosen based on the needs and as per the direction of Govt. of India on National schemes/ 
campaign.
	
l	
Choice of CSR & Sustainability schemes for implementation will preferably be made in consultation/ 
association with the Administrative Authorities of District/ Sub-division/ Blocks/ Panchayats etc. in which 
the NHPC’s Units are operating.
	
l	
Your Company is open to joining hands with the other CPSEs in planning, implementing and monitoring 
of Mega-Projects for optimal use of resources, synergy of expertise and capabilities for maximizing socio-
economic or environmental impact.
	
l	
Any changes in statutory provisions or government guidelines shall be deemed to have been adopted, as 
applicable, in accordance with the provisions issued from time to time.

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment Study of NHPC’s CSR Project titled 
“Improvement/ extension & providing of Water Supply to village Kotla and Theru  
(Ransoo),  Distt. Reasi, J&K”
Access to safe and reliable water remains a critical 
development challenge in rural and hilly regions such 
as District Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir. In response, NHPC 
Limited supported a CSR intervention aimed at improving 
and extending water supply systems in the villages of 
Kotla and Theru (Ransoo) in District Reasi. The project was 
completed in May 2024 at a total expenditure of ₹123.50 
Lakh and was expected to benefit over 600 beneficiaries. 
The project sought to enhance access, reduce the burden 
of water collection, and improve overall quality of life.
This impact assessment study was undertaken to evaluate 
the project’s performance across key dimensions, 
including relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, 
impact, and sustainability, using a mixed-method and 
perception-based SROI approach. The study captures 
beneficiary perspectives to assess not only physical 
outputs but also social value creation.
The assessment was conducted using a structured 
survey across 194 households (Kotla: 98; Theru: 96), 
complemented by field insights and thematic analysis. 
The evaluation framework aligns with the OECD-DAC 
criteria and emphasizes perception-based social returns, 
focusing on dimensions such as access, service reliability, 
quality, implementation experience, and socio-economic 
impact.
Key Findings
l	
Access and Coverage: The project has achieved 
high levels of awareness and village-level coverage, 
with over 90–100% of respondents aware of the 
intervention and acknowledging improved access 
to water sources across their villages. However, 
access remains largely community-based rather 
than household-based. Most households continue 
to rely on shared sources such as springs.
l	
Service Reliability (Critical opportunity area): 
The system is operational and continues to provide 
essential water services to the community. At 
the same time, there is a clear opportunity to 
further strengthen service delivery by improving 
consistency in supply, including aspects such 
as timing, duration, and pressure. Addressing 
occasional disruptions and enhancing system

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment Study 
of NHPC’s CSR Project titled “Modernization of 
Horticulture Nurseries at Khawaja Bagh, Baramulla 
and Baghi Sundari, Sopore in District Baramulla, J&K”
Horticulture is a major livelihood source in District 
Baramulla, Jammu & Kashmir, and the performance of 
local nurseries plays an important role in strengthening 
orchard productivity, access to quality planting material, 
farmer knowledge, and long-term sectoral sustainability. 
In this context, NHPC Limited supported a CSR intervention 
for the modernization of horticulture nurseries at Khawaja 
Bagh, Baramulla, and Baghi Sundari, Sopore, in District 
Baramulla, UT of J&K, which was completed in January 
2025 at an expenditure of ₹142.75 lakh, supporting 362 
beneficiaries, with the objective of improving nursery

infrastructure, enhancing service quality, ensuring the 
availability of planting material, and strengthening 
support to the horticulture ecosystem.
This impact assessment was undertaken to evaluate the 
project’s performance across key dimensions including 
relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability, 
coherence, and perceived social value, using a mixed-
method and perception-based SROI approach. 
The assessment was conducted using a structured 
survey covering 170 respondents across the two nursery 
locations and their stakeholder groups, including 
nursery users, non-users, staff, officials, and community-
linked respondents. The analysis combines descriptive 
interpretation with thematic understanding and aligns 
with the OECD-DAC framework, while incorporating a 
qualitative, perception-based SROI lens to capture non-
monetized social return.

l	
Access, Awareness and Utilization: The project 
has achieved very high awareness and strong 
recent utilization. Most respondents were aware 
of the nursery modernization initiative, and a large 
majority had visited or used nursery services in the 
previous year. However, visit frequency remained 
largely occasional, suggesting that while the 
nurseries are active and visible, repeat engagement 
can still be strengthened. Access was generally 
manageable, though many respondents gave 
neutral responses on ease of access, indicating 
scope to improve service convenience, last-mile 
communication, and seasonal accessibility.
l	
Relevance and Effectiveness: The intervention is 
broadly perceived as relevant to local horticulture 
needs, though relevance intensity is moderate 
rather than exceptionally high. In contrast, the 
effectiveness profile is much stronger. Respondents 
clearly acknowledged improvements in overall

saplings, adequacy of varietal diversity, and timely

one of the strongest findings, particularly in Baghi 
Sundari. These results indicate that the project 
has succeeded in improving the functional core of 
nursery services.

Quality of Planting Material: Perceptions of 
planting material quality are positive overall. Most 
respondents rated the saplings as good or excellent,

These findings are important because they suggest

respondents considered it only slightly useful or 
remained neutral, suggesting that the next stage 
of strengthening should focus on making support 
more practical, targeted, and farmer-responsive.
l	
Implementation Efficiency: The modernization 
initiative is perceived as having been implemented

respondents rated the quality of work as average to 
good, and a majority agreed that implementation 
took place without major operational disruption. 
Negative responses were very limited.

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment 
Study of NHPC’s CSR Project titled “Construction 
of Balika Ashram at Chilli, Tissa, District Chamba, 
Himachal Pradesh”
Girls’ education in remote and hilly regions is often 
constrained by distance, safety concerns, harsh terrain, 
limited transport, and the absence of supportive 
residential infrastructure. In such contexts, access to 
education depends not only on the existence of schools 
but also on the availability of safe, stable, and enabling 
support systems that help girls continue learning with 
dignity and regularity. It is within this developmental 
context that NHPC Limited supported a CSR intervention 
involving the construction of a Balika Ashram at Chilli, 
Tissa, District Chamba, Himachal Pradesh. The project was 
completed in December 2024 at a total expenditure of 
₹4.14 crore catering to 50 beneficiaries. The initiative aims 
to enhance girls’ access to safe residential facilities, ensure 
continuity of education, and promote their overall well-
being in a geographically challenging region.
This impact assessment was undertaken to evaluate the 
project’s performance across key dimensions including 
relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability, 
coherence, and perceived social value, using a mixed-
method and perception-based SROI approach. The 
analysis aligns with the OECD-DAC framework and 
incorporates a qualitative, perception-based SROI lens to 
capture non-monetized educational and social return.
The assessment was conducted using a structured survey 
covering 92 respondents, dominated by student/ residents 
and supported by a smaller share of staff respondents. 
The analysis combines descriptive interpretation with 
thematic synthesis and is supplemented by stakeholder 
suggestions, student perspectives, and open-ended 
reflections on positive change and improvement needs.
Key Findings
l	
Access, Relevance and Need: The project is 
perceived as highly relevant to local needs. 
Respondents overwhelmingly agreed that the 
Balika Ashram addressed a genuine requirement 
for girls’ educational support and was particularly 
important for girls from remote and hilly villages. 
Admission and selection processes were also widely 
viewed as fair and transparent, and the intervention 
was seen as supportive of girls from economically 
weaker sections. These findings indicate that the 
project enjoys strong local legitimacy and is seen 
as a meaningful response to educational-access 
barriers in the project geography.
l	
Facilities and Basic Services: The facilities 
profile is strongly positive. Respondents rated 
the overall building facilities, toilets, bathing 
arrangements, and electricity/lighting as largely 
good or excellent. Drinking water availability 
and cleanliness/housekeeping received universal 
positive responses. Waste management, drainage, 
environmental cleanliness, and green surroundings 
were also viewed favorably. These findings show 
that the Balika Ashram is functioning not merely as 
a completed structure but as a usable and generally 
well-maintained residential facility.
l	
Safety, Dignity and Grievance Systems: One of the 
strongest result areas in the assessment relates to 
safety and dignity. Respondents reported very high 
confidence that girls feel safe within the premises, 
that their privacy and dignity are respected, that 
a clear grievance or complaint system exists, and 
that issues reported are responded to in a timely 
manner. This indicates that the Ashram is perceived 
not only as physically secure, but also as socially and 
institutionally supportive of girls’ dignity and well-
being.
l	
Education and Outcomes: The education and 
outcomes profile is highly positive. Respondents 
overwhelmingly agreed that the Ashram has 
improved regular school attendance, supported 
a 
structured 
learning 
environment, 
reduced 
dropout risk, and improved the overall quality 
of life and well-being of girls. These findings 
suggest that the intervention is functioning not 
merely as accommodation, but as a meaningful 
educational support mechanism that helps girls 
remain connected to schooling in a more stable and 
organized way.

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment Study 
of NHPC’s CSR Project titled “Employment-Oriented 
Vocational Training of 4000 Youth”
Employment-oriented vocational training has emerged 
as an important CSR intervention for improving youth 
employability, supporting livelihood diversification, and 
enhancing socio-economic inclusion in geographically 
dispersed and opportunity-constrained regions. In 
this context, NHPC Limited supported a CSR initiative 
relating to Employment Oriented Vocational Training 
for 4000 youth through NSDC/NSDF for promoting skill 
development, implemented across locations in Jammu 
& Kashmir, Ladakh, Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh, Assam, 
West Bengal, Uttarakhand, Manipur, and Arunachal 
Pradesh. The project was completed in 2024 with a total 
expenditure of ₹796.92 lakh and 4000 youth beneficiaries. 
This impact assessment study was undertaken to 
evaluate the project’s performance across key dimensions 
including relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, 
impact, and sustainability, using a mixed-method and 
perception-based SROI approach. The assessment 
captures beneficiary experience not only in terms of 
training delivery, but also in relation to employability, 
self-employment, livelihood improvement, inclusion, 
and perceived social value. The evaluation framework 
is aligned with the OECD-DAC criteria and emphasizes 
perception-based social returns, focusing on dimensions 
such as training relevance, skill improvement, training 
quality, placement and self-employment outcomes, 
income change, community value, and long-term 
sustainability.
The assessment was conducted using a structured survey 
covering 643 respondents, supported by regrouped 
thematic interpretation of open-ended responses and 
policy-oriented analysis. The respondent profile indicates 
that the programme largely reached its intended

sizeable neutral segment suggests that certification 
alone did not guarantee livelihood conversion in

linkage between certification and labour-market 
opportunities.

and

Outcomes: One of the strongest findings of the

programme contributed meaningfully to livelihood 
generation through more than one pathway. Most 
respondents also reported some degree of increase 
in household income compared to the pre-training 
period.
At the same time, some notable concerns remain 
visible. Formal placement support was reported by 
only a minority of respondents, and trade-to-job 
alignment was only moderate, with a significant 
share working outside their training domain. Income 
levels were concentrated largely in lower to mid-
level bands, and job satisfaction was more often 
neutral than strongly positive. This suggests that 
while the programme succeeded in enabling work 
entry, it was less consistent in ensuring stronger 
job quality, higher incomes, or direct trade-specific 
placement.

Self-Employment and Enterprise Support: Self-
employment emerged as a major pathway, with 
many respondents reporting that the programme 
helped them reduce dependence on seasonal 
or informal work and enabled them to start a 
business or self-employment activity. However, 
entrepreneurship support in the form of toolkits, 
credit linkage, or business guidance was reported by

were 
achieved 
despite 
relatively 
limited enterprise-enabling support, pointing to a 
opportunity area in the post-training ecosystem.

Outcomes: Beyond livelihood entry, the programme

A majority of respondents reported improved 
financial independence, stronger ability to support 
their family, and enhanced social confidence and 
community standing. Respondents also perceived 
the programme as contributing to reduction in 
youth unemployment, improvement in community 
perception towards skill-based employment, and 
creation of local livelihood opportunities. A large 
majority further believed that local employers and 
businesses benefited from the availability of trained 
youth. These findings indicate that the intervention 
created value not only at the individual level, but 
also at the community and local economy level.

Equity and Inclusion: The programme was 
broadly perceived as inclusive. Most respondents

were able to participate effectively, that the 
programme contributed positively to gender 
equality and women’s opportunities, and that it 
encouraged the participation of marginalized and 
economically weaker groups. However, several 
participation barriers remained visible, especially 
distance/transport, lack of awareness, costs, family 
restrictions, course timing, and safety concerns. This 
indicates that while the programme was inclusive in 
design and perception, access constraints were not 
fully eliminated.
l	
Efficiency: The programme was generally perceived 
as having been implemented efficiently in terms 
of mobilisation, scheduling, and coordination. 
Most respondents believed that implementation 
quality was strong and that no major delays 
affected outcomes. However, a sizeable minority 
did indicate that delays or issues had affected the 
training experience, suggesting that efficiency was 
high overall but not completely uniform across all 
locations.
l	
Sustainability: The sustainability findings present 
a mixed but promising picture. More than half of 
respondents felt that they were likely to continue 
working or earning using these skills over the next 
1–2 years. However, a sizeable group remained 
uncertain, and many identified the need for 
continued support in the form of placement follow-
up, advanced training, toolkit/equipment support, 
market linkages, and credit support. This suggests 
that while the programme created a positive 
foundation, long-term sustainability depends on 
stronger post-training support systems.

socially valuable. A majority of respondents viewed

and the community, most believed that the money

majority said they would recommend similar skill

strong perception-based social returns and high

Coherence and Stakeholder Recommendations:

aligned with broader government skill development 
initiatives such as Skill India and PMKVY. At the 
same time, stakeholder suggestions indicate clear 
expectations for future strengthening. The most 
prominent needs were better placement support, 
financial support/credit linkage, advanced training, 
toolkits/equipment support, practical exposure, 
and accessible training arrangements. This suggests

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment Study 
of NHPC’s CSR Project titled “Construction of 5th Floor 
of Laghu Udyog Bharati Multi Skill Development 
Centre at Jaipur, Rajasthan”
Skill 
development 
infrastructure 
plays 
a 
critical 
role in improving access to training, strengthening 
institutional capacity, and supporting employability-
oriented learning. In many contexts, the effectiveness of 
skilling initiatives depends not only on course delivery 
but also on the availability of adequate space, usable 
classrooms and labs, basic utilities, learner comfort, and 
supportive institutional systems. It is within this broader 
developmental context that NHPC Limited supported 
a CSR intervention for the construction of the fifth floor 
of the Laghu Udyog Bharati Multi Skill Development 
Centre in Jaipur, Rajasthan, at an expenditure of ₹112.58 
lakh, supporting 1000 beneficiaries, with the objective 
of strengthening training infrastructure, enhancing 
institutional capacity, and improving the overall quality of 
the learning environment.
This impact assessment was undertaken to evaluate the 
project’s performance across key dimensions including 
relevance, 
effectiveness, 
efficiency, 
sustainability, 
coherence, and perceived social value, using a mixed-
method and perception-based approach. The analysis is 
aligned with the OECD-DAC framework and incorporates 
a qualitative, perception-based SROI lens to capture non-
monetized value in terms of institutional strengthening, 
learner experience, and support to future employability. 
The assessment was conducted using a structured survey 
covering 175 respondents, dominated by trainees/ 
students (96.0%), with a smaller share of trainers/faculty 
and centre management/staff. The respondent base was 
strongly female-dominated and heavily concentrated in 
the 18–30 years category, indicating that the findings are 
grounded mainly in the perceptions of young direct users 
of the expanded facility. The course profile reflected both 
traditional and emerging skill domains, led by Fashion, 
Garment & Design, followed by Digital Marketing, 
Advanced Excel / Office Applications, and AI / Basic AI. 
Awareness of NHPC’s CSR support was moderate to high.
Key Findings
l	
Access, Relevance and Need: The infrastructure 
expansion is widely perceived as relevant to the 
needs of the centre and its users. A clear majority 
of 
respondents 
considered 
the 
intervention 
relevant or highly relevant for improving skill 
training facilities in Jaipur. Positive responses were 
especially strong regarding improvement in overall 
infrastructure and space availability, increased 
training capacity, and regular functional use of the 
5th floor. These findings suggest that the project 
addressed a genuine institutional need and enjoys 
strong functional legitimacy among users.
l	
Training Environment and Facility Quality: 
The facility-quality profile is broadly positive. 
Respondents 
rated 
classrooms, 
labs, 
and 
workspaces, as well as lighting, ventilation, seating, 
cleanliness, toilets, drinking water, safety provisions, 
and equipment adequacy largely as good or 
excellent. The strongest responses were recorded 
for cleanliness, basic services, and safety provisions. 
At the same time, a meaningful “average” segment 
was visible across several indicators, indicating 
that while the facility is clearly functional and 
appreciated, users now expect further improvement 
in comfort, refinement, and course-specific support.
l	
Efficiency, Usability and Operational Readiness: 
The implementation quality profile is also positive. 
Most respondents rated construction quality as 
durable and in line with standards, and a majority 
felt that the facility was completed and made usable 
without major delays or disruption. Perceptions 
of utility readiness—such as electricity, water, 
and furnishings—were particularly strong. These 
results indicate that the intervention has moved 
successfully beyond construction completion and is 
functioning as a usable institutional asset. However, 
the sizeable average-rated group on construction 
quality and completion readiness suggests that 
operational refinement and user confidence can still 
be improved.
l	
Outcomes Enabled: One of the strongest result 
areas in the assessment relates to outcomes 
enabled 
by 
the 
infrastructure. 
Respondents 
overwhelmingly 
agreed 
that 
the 
improved 
facility has enhanced training quality and learner 
experience, strengthened the centre’s ability to offer 
more diverse courses and trades, and contributed 
to better employability support through placement 
guidance, counselling, and exposure. This indicates 
that the 5th floor is being experienced not merely as 
added built-up area, but as a platform that improves 
the functional capability of the institution.

a more complete and better-supported skilling 
ecosystem.

outcomes. Most importantly, an overwhelming 
majority recommended similar CSR support for 
skill infrastructure in other locations. This indicates 
strong practical acceptability, high perceived public 
value, and significant replication potential.

Executive Summary of the Impact Assessment Study of 
NHPC’s CSR Project titled “Construction of Community 
Halls in 3 villages of Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh”
In many rural settings, the effectiveness of local 
governance, community participation, public service 
delivery, and collective social action depends not only on 
the presence of institutions, but also on the availability 
of functional and accessible common-use infrastructure. 
In such contexts, community halls serve as important 
shared public assets that support Gram Sabha meetings, 
SHG activities, trainings, awareness programmes, cultural 
events, social gatherings, and village-level coordination. 
It is within this developmental context that NHPC Limited 
supported the Community Hall Construction Initiative in 
three villages of Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh—namely 
Angaluru, Tarakaturu, and Thotlavalluru—by constructing 
one community hall in each village, at a total expenditure 
of ₹135.58 lakh, supporting 7843 beneficiaries, with 
the broader objective of improving access to shared 
community infrastructure and strengthening village-level 
participation and development processes. 
This impact assessment was undertaken to evaluate the 
project’s performance across key dimensions including 
relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability, 
coherence, and perceived social value, using a mixed-
method and perception-based SROI approach. The 
assessment goes beyond physical outputs and focuses 
on how beneficiaries and associated stakeholders 
perceive the project’s functional utility, developmental 
contribution, and social value. The analysis aligns with 
the OECD-DAC framework and incorporates a qualitative 
approach to capture non-monetized community and 
developmental returns. 
The assessment was conducted using a structured survey 
covering 189 respondents, supported by qualitative 
insights from open-ended responses, KIIs, FGDs, and 
observation-based evidence. The respondent base was 
largely composed of local residents and was reasonably 
distributed across the three village locations, allowing the 
findings to reflect broad community-level perceptions of 
the intervention.
Key Findings
l	
Access, Relevance and Need: The project is 
perceived as broadly relevant to local needs. A 
majority of respondents rated the halls as relevant 
or highly relevant, and very high proportions 
agreed that the halls improved the village’s ability 
to conduct meetings and community programmes. 
Respondents also reported very strong perceptions 
of accessibility and fairness of access for women, 
elderly persons, and persons with disabilities. These 
findings indicate that the project enjoys strong local 

128

legitimacy and is seen as a meaningful response to 
the need for common village-level infrastructure.
l	
Utilisation and Access: The halls are actively used, 
though use is more strongly occasional than highly 
regular. The most common reported uses include 
Gram Sabha meetings, trainings and awareness 
programmes, cultural events, functions, SHG 
meetings, and health camps. A strong majority 
of respondents also reported that the booking 
or permission process is clear and that access is 
fair for all groups. This indicates that the halls are 
functioning as accessible public-use spaces, though 
the intensity and regularity of use can still deepen 
over time.
l	
Facility 
Quality 
and 
Basic 
Services: 
The 
infrastructure

Respondents rated overall construction quality

adequacy, and utility availability as largely good

availability, while adequate, present scope for 
further strengthening relative to the rest of the 
infrastructure profile, indicating that the facility is 
usable and broadly serviceable, with opportunities 
to achieve greater uniformity across all amenity 
dimensions.
l	
Community Outcomes: The halls are perceived as 
generating meaningful community-level effects. 
Large majorities of respondents agreed that the 
halls have increased community participation 
in meetings and programmes, supported better 
delivery of government/community services such as 
meetings, camps, and trainings, and strengthened 
social cohesion and collective decision-making. 
Overall satisfaction with the hall is positive. This 
suggests that the halls are functioning as socially 
useful and institutionally relevant public platforms.
l	
Sustainability and Long-Term Usability: The 
sustainability profile is highly encouraging. Most 
respondents reported that the halls are maintained 
regularly and that maintenance responsibility is led 
mainly by Gram Panchayat/PRI structures, followed 
by village committees and other forms of support. 
A large majority also reported the presence of 
some fund, user charge, or booking-based system 
that supports maintenance. Most importantly, 
respondents expressed very high confidence that 
the halls will remain functional and beneficial over 
the next 3–5 years. These findings indicate that 
the intervention has moved beyond asset creation 
and is functioning as a locally supported and 
operationally sustainable village asset.
l	
Environmental Sustainability: The environmental 
profile is broadly positive. Most respondents 
confirmed the presence of waste management 
arrangements, 
energy-efficient 
measures, 
environmental cleanliness, and green surroundings 
around the halls. A particularly strong outcome 
is the use of halls for environmental awareness 
activities such as cleanliness drives and plantation 
campaigns. In addition, drainage and wastewater 
disposal have received steady ratings, reflecting 
that while environmental responsibility is well 
integrated overall, there remains scope to further 
enhance consistency in environmental service 
quality across locations.
l	
Community Value and Extended Local Outcomes: 
One of the stronger findings of the assessment 
is that the halls are creating value beyond basic 
infrastructure. Large majorities reported that the 
halls are used for educational or skill-development 
programmes, support collective issue resolution 
through discussions and meetings, reduce the 
cost of renting private venues, and support local 
economic activities such as trainings, SHG meetings, 
and livelihood workshops. Respondents also 
acknowledged benefits to local vendors and service 
providers during events. These findings indicate 
that the halls are generating both social and local 
economic spillover value.
l	
Coherence and Stakeholder Suggestions: The 
coherence profile is very strong. Most respondents 
felt that the halls align very well or moderately 
well with local governance and community 
development needs. The open-ended improvement 
suggestions are also highly coherent: respondents 
are not rejecting the intervention, but asking for a 
stronger second phase of strengthening. The most 
repeated suggestions include toilet and washroom 
facilities, drinking water, completion of pending 
infrastructure, hall expansion, better maintenance 
and cleanliness, more equipment, improved 
ventilation or cooling, and clearer management 
or booking systems. This indicates that the 
project is directionally successful, and community 
expectations are now moving toward quality 
enhancement and fuller usability.

of respondents directly described the project as

segment remained cautious in assigning stronger 
value intensity. At the same time, a strong majority 
believed that the money spent was justified, and

Conclusion and Way Forward
The NHPC-supported Community Hall initiative in 
Krishna District has made a meaningful contribution to 
improving shared public infrastructure, participation, 
public programme support, community coordination, 
environmental awareness use, and local social-economic 
value. The project demonstrates strong relevance, 
satisfactory effectiveness, positive infrastructure usability, 
encouraging sustainability potential, and strong practical 
social value. Most importantly, it is widely regarded as a 
model worth sustaining and replicating.
While the project has successfully delivered functional 
infrastructure and created meaningful community utility, 
there is considerable potential to further strengthen 
its evolution into a fully developed, regularly activated, 
development-oriented, and uniformly maintained public-
use system. Continued attention to enhancing toilet 
and water facilities, completing pending components, 
expanding capacity where required, ensuring routine 
maintenance, promoting environmental consistency, and 
deepening programme activation will help unlock its full 
long-term value.
The initiative has laid a strong foundation in terms of 
infrastructure creation and community benefit. Its overall 
impact can be further amplified through more consistent 
developmental use, greater completeness of amenities, 
deeper integration with local institutions, and sustained 
focus on maintenance and management quality.
The Community Hall Construction Initiative aligns closely 
with several United Nations Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and 
Communities) by creating inclusive, safe, and accessible 
public spaces that support community interaction and 
local governance. The initiative also contributes to SDG 16 
(Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) by strengthening 
platforms for participatory decision-making, Gram Sabha 
engagement, and collective problem-solving at the village 
level. Further, by enabling the use of halls for training 
programmes, awareness campaigns, SHG meetings, 
and skill development activities, the project supports 
SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 8 (Decent Work 
and Economic Growth) through capacity building and 
livelihood-related engagement. The focus on inclusive 
access for women, elderly persons, and vulnerable groups

Regulations and Section 149(1) of the Companies

and the Nomination & Remuneration Committee

3.1.2 of DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance.

meeting.

were carried out unanimously or through requisite 
majority as recorded in the minutes of the meetings of the 
Board of Directors or respective Committee of the Board, 
as the case may be.
There was no prosecution initiated during the year under 
review against/ on the Company, its Directors and Officers. 
However, during the year under review, BSE Limited (BSE) 
and National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE) each 
have imposed fine on the Company for non-compliance 
of Regulation 17(1), 18(1) and 19(1)/19(2) of the SEBI 
Listing Regulations for various quarters during FY 2025-
26 in respect of non-appointment of requisite number of 
independent directors (including woman independent 
Director) and composition of Audit Committee and 
Nomination & Remuneration Committee. In response to 
the notices, the Company has clarified to the Exchanges 
that the shortfall in independent directors was not 
due to any negligence/ default of the Company, as 
the appointment is not within control of Board or the 
Company. In view thereof, the Company has requested 
the Exchanges to waive-off the fine under their carve-
out policies. Considering justification submitted by the 
Company for waiver of fines, NSE & BSE has waived-off all 
the fines imposed under Regulation 18(1) and 19(1) for 
quarter ended 30.06.2025.
